analysis.one_liner: Bans organophosphate pesticide residues from all food sold in the US.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban organophosphate pesticides from food never got a vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee from August 2022 until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for any food to contain an organophosphate pesticide or its residue — a class of neurotoxic bug killers linked to nerve damage, especially in farmworkers and children. It would close a loophole by overriding any legal "tolerance" the EPA had set for these chemicals. The bill was introduced in August 2022, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, especially children, whose food would no longer carry organophosphate residues; farmworkers and rural residents most exposed to these pesticides through spraying, drift, and handling; and the EPA's own regulatory staff, who would get a clearer statutory floor. The EPA had already banned one organophosphate, chlorpyrifos, from food in February 2022, and this bill would have made that kind of ban permanent and universal across the whole class of chemicals.

how_it_helps.text: Makes any food containing an organophosphate pesticide or its residue legally adulterated, banning the entire class of neurotoxic pesticides from food regardless of the EPA's tolerance levels.

Protects people most exposed to organophosphates — farmworkers who handle and spray them and families eating treated produce — from chemicals linked to neurological harm, with children especially sensitive.
Locks in and extends the EPA's own 2022 ban on chlorpyrifos by covering every organophosphate, so future administrations could not quietly re-approve a neurotoxic pesticide for food use.

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers who sell organophosphates, and the growers of fruits, vegetables, and other crops that would have to switch to alternative pest-control methods or absorb losses from reduced yields. Those costs would partly flow to consumers as higher produce prices in the short run.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pesticide makers and farmers who use them

drawbacks.text: Growers of crops where organophosphates are the effective or affordable option — like certain fruits, vegetables, and specialty crops — would face higher pest-control costs or lower yields, and some of that cost would reach shoppers as higher produce prices.

The bill bans by chemical class rather than by measured risk, so it would also prohibit organophosphates where residue levels are low; supporters would argue that fits the science on neurotoxins, but it goes beyond what the EPA's own tolerances allowed for some uses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health benefit is real and well-documented — organophosphates are nerve agents in agricultural form, and children and farmworkers bear the exposure — but the bill was written as a flat class-wide ban without transition support for growers. The main reason it died was not a fair fight over that trade-off: it never received any committee action at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up before the two-year Congress ended, so it died there.

narrative.text: Rep. Nydia Velazquez introduced the bill on August 30, 2022, joined by eight original cosponsors and eventually 14 Democrats in total.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which holds jurisdiction over food and pesticide safety.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed; the bill's action history ends with the committee referral, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide manufacturers and growers who rely on organophosphates are better off, because the class-wide ban never advanced and no committee even considered it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pesticide makers and growers who use them

for.name: Rep. Nydia Velazquez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 14 Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 14 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; all 14 cosponsors were Democrats, so the bill never drew the broader support needed to reach the floor.

industries.note: The bill would have eliminated their food-use market for the entire class, building on the EPA's 2022 chlorpyrifos ban. Because the bill died in committee, they lost nothing and their products remain on the market wherever tolerances allow.

Growers who use organophosphates would have faced higher pest-control costs or lower yields and would have had to switch to alternatives. Their interest in keeping current tools runs against the public's interest in residue-free food, though many already faced pressure from the chlorpyrifos ban.
